title: Quality Control & Assurance
source_note: Grounded in standard NUC-aligned quality control and quality assurance curricula for laboratory technology programmes: QC/QA fundamentals, statistical control, calibration and traceability, SOPs, ISO/GLP frameworks, and documentation practices.

questions.question: What is the key distinction between Quality Control (QC) and Quality Assurance (QA)?
options: QC is product/output-focused testing to detect defects, while QA is a system of planned processes to prevent defects
QC and QA mean exactly the same thing in a laboratory
QA is only performed after a product is sold to the customer
QC applies only to finished goods, while QA applies only to raw materials
questions.correct_answer: QC is product/output-focused testing to detect defects, while QA is a system of planned processes to prevent defects
questions.explanation: QC involves inspecting/testing outputs to identify defects, whereas QA is the broader, proactive system of procedures designed to prevent defects from occurring in the first place.

questions.question: Accuracy in a measurement system refers to:
options: How close a measured value is to the true or accepted value
How close repeated measurements are to each other
The number of decimal places an instrument can display
The speed at which a measurement is taken
questions.correct_answer: How close a measured value is to the true or accepted value
questions.explanation: Accuracy describes the closeness of a measured result to the true/reference value, distinguishing it from precision, which describes reproducibility.

questions.question: Precision in a measurement system refers to:
options: How close repeated measurements of the same quantity are to one another
How close a single measurement is to the true value
The cost of the measuring instrument
The brand of the instrument used
questions.correct_answer: How close repeated measurements of the same quantity are to one another
questions.explanation: Precision reflects the reproducibility/consistency of repeated measurements, regardless of whether they are close to the true value (accuracy).

questions.question: A set of measurements that are tightly clustered together but far from the true value is described as:
options: Precise but not accurate
Accurate but not precise
Both accurate and precise
Neither accurate nor precise
questions.correct_answer: Precise but not accurate
questions.explanation: Tight clustering indicates high precision (low random error), while being far from the true value indicates poor accuracy (likely due to systematic/bias error).

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of calibrating a laboratory instrument such as a weighing balance or pH meter?
options: To verify and adjust the instrument's readings against a known reference standard, ensuring accuracy
To make the instrument run faster
To permanently fix any mechanical damage to the instrument
To change the instrument's model number
questions.correct_answer: To verify and adjust the instrument's readings against a known reference standard, ensuring accuracy
questions.explanation: Calibration compares an instrument's output to a traceable reference standard and adjusts or documents any deviation, ensuring measurement accuracy over time.

questions.question: What does 'traceability' mean in a laboratory measurement context?
options: An unbroken chain of calibrations linking a measurement result back to a recognized (e.g. national or international) reference standard
The ability to trace who used an instrument last
Recording only the final result of an experiment
The physical location of the laboratory
questions.correct_answer: An unbroken chain of calibrations linking a measurement result back to a recognized (e.g. national or international) reference standard
questions.explanation: Metrological traceability requires a documented, unbroken chain of comparisons connecting a measurement to a higher-level reference standard, ensuring reliability and comparability of results.

questions.question: A Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) in a laboratory is best defined as:
options: A documented, step-by-step set of instructions for performing a specific task consistently
A general company mission statement
An informal verbal agreement between staff on how to work
A one-time memo issued for a single experiment
questions.correct_answer: A documented, step-by-step set of instructions for performing a specific task consistently
questions.explanation: SOPs are formal written documents that standardize how a task is performed, ensuring consistency, repeatability, and compliance across different operators and times.

questions.question: Why are SOPs important for maintaining quality in a laboratory setting?
options: They reduce variability between operators and ensure procedures are performed consistently every time
They eliminate the need for staff training entirely
They are only required for financial audits
They replace the need for any instrument calibration
questions.correct_answer: They reduce variability between operators and ensure procedures are performed consistently every time
questions.explanation: SOPs standardize methods so that results are reproducible regardless of which trained technician performs the procedure, reducing process variation.

questions.question: In statistical process control (SPC), a control chart is primarily used to:
options: Monitor a process over time and distinguish between normal (common-cause) variation and abnormal (special-cause) variation
Record employee attendance
Calculate the final invoice for a client
Design the layout of the laboratory
questions.correct_answer: Monitor a process over time and distinguish between normal (common-cause) variation and abnormal (special-cause) variation
questions.explanation: Control charts plot process data over time against upper and lower control limits, helping identify when a process has drifted out of statistical control due to a special cause.

questions.question: On a standard Shewhart control chart, the control limits are typically set at:
options: The process mean plus or minus 3 standard deviations
The process mean plus or minus 1 standard deviation
The absolute minimum and maximum values ever recorded
Exactly the specification limits set by the customer
questions.correct_answer: The process mean plus or minus 3 standard deviations
questions.explanation: Conventional control charts set upper and lower control limits at the mean ± 3 standard deviations, capturing about 99.7% of data from a stable process under normal variation.

questions.question: A data point falling outside the control limits on a control chart most likely indicates:
options: The presence of a special (assignable) cause of variation that should be investigated
That the process is perfectly in control
That the instrument needs to be replaced with a cheaper one
That no further action is required
questions.correct_answer: The presence of a special (assignable) cause of variation that should be investigated
questions.explanation: Points outside control limits signal that variation is likely due to an identifiable, assignable cause rather than normal random process variation, warranting investigation.

questions.question: What is meant by 'tolerance' in a quality control specification for a manufactured item?
options: The permissible range of variation around a target value that is still considered acceptable
The exact single value a product must have with no deviation allowed
The number of defective products allowed per year
The cost allowance for producing the item
questions.correct_answer: The permissible range of variation around a target value that is still considered acceptable
questions.explanation: Tolerance defines the acceptable upper and lower deviation from a nominal/target specification within which a product is still considered to meet quality requirements.

questions.question: In quality control, sampling refers to:
options: Selecting a representative subset of items or material from a larger batch/population for testing
Testing every single unit produced without exception
Discarding all test results after use
Only weighing raw materials before production
questions.correct_answer: Selecting a representative subset of items or material from a larger batch/population for testing
questions.explanation: Sampling involves choosing a representative portion of a lot for inspection or testing, since testing 100% of items (destructive testing especially) is often impractical.

questions.question: Why is random sampling generally preferred over convenience sampling in quality control testing?
options: It reduces selection bias and gives every unit in the batch an equal chance of being tested, making the sample more representative
It is always faster than any other sampling method
It guarantees zero defects will be found
It requires no statistical justification
questions.correct_answer: It reduces selection bias and gives every unit in the batch an equal chance of being tested, making the sample more representative
questions.explanation: Random sampling minimizes bias by giving each unit equal selection probability, producing a sample that better reflects the true characteristics of the whole batch.

questions.question: ISO 9001 is an international standard primarily concerned with:
options: Quality management systems for organizations
Environmental management systems only
Food safety management exclusively
Information security management exclusively
questions.correct_answer: Quality management systems for organizations
questions.explanation: ISO 9001 specifies requirements for a quality management system, helping organizations consistently provide products/services that meet customer and regulatory requirements.

questions.question: ISO/IEC 17025 is the international standard specifically for:
options: The general competence of testing and calibration laboratories
Food packaging design
Corporate financial auditing
Building construction safety
questions.correct_answer: The general competence of testing and calibration laboratories
questions.explanation: ISO/IEC 17025 specifies the general requirements for the competence, impartiality, and consistent operation of testing and calibration laboratories.

questions.question: Good Laboratory Practice (GLP) is best described as:
options: A quality system covering the organizational process and conditions under which non-clinical studies are planned, performed, monitored, and reported
A rule that laboratories must be painted white
A set of instructions only for cleaning glassware
A voluntary suggestion with no formal documentation required
questions.correct_answer: A quality system covering the organizational process and conditions under which non-clinical studies are planned, performed, monitored, and reported
questions.explanation: GLP is a formal quality system governing the organization and conduct of laboratory studies to ensure the reliability, traceability, and integrity of generated data.

questions.question: In a quality management system, what is a 'non-conformance'?
options: A deviation from a specified requirement, standard, or procedure
A document listing employee salaries
A type of calibration certificate
A scheduled routine maintenance task
questions.correct_answer: A deviation from a specified requirement, standard, or procedure
questions.explanation: A non-conformance is any instance where a product, process, or result fails to meet a defined requirement, specification, or documented procedure.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a corrective action in a quality system after a non-conformance is identified?
options: To eliminate the root cause of the problem and prevent its recurrence
To hide the non-conformance from auditors
To immediately shut down the entire laboratory permanently
To increase production speed regardless of the defect
questions.correct_answer: To eliminate the root cause of the problem and prevent its recurrence
questions.explanation: Corrective action investigates and addresses the underlying root cause of a non-conformance, distinguishing it from a mere quick fix, to prevent the problem recurring.

questions.question: What is the difference between a corrective action and a preventive action in quality management?
options: Corrective action addresses a problem that has already occurred, while preventive action addresses a potential problem before it occurs
They are identical terms with no distinction
Preventive action can only be taken after a customer complaint
Corrective action is always cheaper than preventive action
questions.correct_answer: Corrective action addresses a problem that has already occurred, while preventive action addresses a potential problem before it occurs
questions.explanation: Corrective action is reactive, fixing an existing non-conformance and its cause; preventive action is proactive, addressing potential future non-conformances before they happen.

questions.question: An internal quality audit in a laboratory is conducted primarily to:
options: Independently verify that the laboratory's activities comply with its own quality system and relevant standards
Increase the number of samples tested per day
Reduce the number of staff employed
Advertise the laboratory to new clients
questions.correct_answer: Independently verify that the laboratory's activities comply with its own quality system and relevant standards
questions.explanation: Internal audits systematically and independently review whether documented procedures are being followed and whether the quality system is effective, identifying gaps for improvement.

questions.question: Why must all laboratory test results, calculations, and observations be recorded in real time, in ink, in a bound notebook or validated electronic system (rather than on loose scrap paper)?
options: To ensure data integrity, traceability, and an auditable, tamper-evident record
Because loose paper is more expensive
Because scrap paper cannot hold liquid spills
It has no bearing on data quality, only tidiness
questions.correct_answer: To ensure data integrity, traceability, and an auditable, tamper-evident record
questions.explanation: Contemporaneous, permanent recordkeeping (a key GLP/data-integrity principle) prevents data loss, supports traceability, and provides an auditable record that cannot be easily altered.

questions.question: The 'ALCOA' principles used to assess data integrity in quality systems stand for data that is:
options: Attributable, Legible, Contemporaneous, Original, Accurate
Available, Long-lasting, Colourful, Organized, Affordable
Accurate, Legal, Complete, Official, Approved
Automated, Localized, Compressed, Optimized, Archived
questions.correct_answer: Attributable, Legible, Contemporaneous, Original, Accurate
questions.explanation: ALCOA is a widely used data integrity framework requiring that data be Attributable, Legible, Contemporaneous, Original, and Accurate.

questions.question: In quality control terminology, what is a 'Certificate of Analysis' (CoA)?
options: A document confirming that a batch of product or material meets specified quality requirements, based on actual test results
A certificate awarded to an employee for good attendance
A marketing brochure for a new product
A record of laboratory electricity consumption
questions.correct_answer: A document confirming that a batch of product or material meets specified quality requirements, based on actual test results
questions.explanation: A Certificate of Analysis lists the actual test results for specified quality parameters of a batch, confirming it conforms to the required specification.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes 'measurement uncertainty'?
options: A quantified doubt about the validity of a measurement result, expressing the range within which the true value likely lies
The complete absence of any error in a measurement
The list of instruments used in an experiment
The cost of purchasing a new measuring instrument
questions.correct_answer: A quantified doubt about the validity of a measurement result, expressing the range within which the true value likely lies
questions.explanation: Measurement uncertainty is a parameter associated with a measurement result that characterizes the dispersion of values that could reasonably be attributed to the measured quantity.

questions.question: In quality control, what is the purpose of using a 'reference standard' or 'certified reference material' (CRM)?
options: To validate the accuracy of test methods and instruments against a material with a known, certified property value
To decorate the laboratory shelf
To replace the need for any SOPs
To act as a disposable cleaning agent
questions.correct_answer: To validate the accuracy of test methods and instruments against a material with a known, certified property value
questions.explanation: A CRM has an accurately known and certified value, allowing laboratories to check the accuracy of their methods and instruments by comparison.

questions.question: What does 'batch' or 'lot' mean in a quality control context for manufactured or processed materials?
options: A defined quantity of material produced in a single process run, assumed to have uniform characteristics
The total annual output of a factory
A single unit of finished product
The name of the quality control department
questions.correct_answer: A defined quantity of material produced in a single process run, assumed to have uniform characteristics
questions.explanation: A batch/lot is produced under conditions considered uniform, so a sample from it is assumed representative of the entire batch for quality testing purposes.

questions.question: Which of these best describes the role of Statistical Process Control (SPC) in preventing defects, compared to end-of-line inspection alone?
options: SPC monitors the process in real time so problems can be corrected before large quantities of defective product are made
SPC only inspects the final finished product after it is completed
SPC eliminates the need for any process monitoring
SPC is only applicable to service industries, never manufacturing
questions.correct_answer: SPC monitors the process in real time so problems can be corrected before large quantities of defective product are made
questions.explanation: SPC shifts quality control 'upstream' by tracking the process itself in real time, allowing early detection and correction of drift before large-scale defects accumulate.

questions.question: What is meant by 'repeatability' when validating a test method?
options: The closeness of agreement between results of successive measurements of the same sample, by the same operator, using the same equipment, under the same conditions, in a short time interval
The ability of a method to work in any laboratory worldwide
How quickly a test can be completed
The shelf-life of the reagents used
questions.correct_answer: The closeness of agreement between results of successive measurements of the same sample, by the same operator, using the same equipment, under the same conditions, in a short time interval
questions.explanation: Repeatability specifically measures precision under the same, unchanged conditions (same analyst, equipment, lab, short timeframe), distinguishing it from reproducibility (different conditions/labs).

questions.question: What is 'reproducibility' in method validation, as distinct from repeatability?
options: The closeness of agreement between results obtained under changed conditions, such as different operators, equipment, or laboratories
The exact same meaning as repeatability
The number of times an experiment must be repeated by law
A measure of instrument cost
questions.correct_answer: The closeness of agreement between results obtained under changed conditions, such as different operators, equipment, or laboratories
questions.explanation: Reproducibility assesses precision when one or more conditions are varied (e.g. different analyst, instrument, or lab), unlike repeatability which holds conditions constant.

questions.question: In quality control, what is the purpose of maintaining an equipment calibration schedule/log?
options: To ensure instruments are calibrated at defined intervals so measurement accuracy and traceability are maintained over time
To track how much electricity each instrument consumes
To decide which instruments to discard at the end of the year regardless of condition
To satisfy an insurance requirement only, with no scientific benefit
questions.correct_answer: To ensure instruments are calibrated at defined intervals so measurement accuracy and traceability are maintained over time
questions.explanation: Scheduled, documented calibration ensures instruments remain within acceptable accuracy limits and that this can be demonstrated as part of traceability and quality assurance.

questions.question: A weighing balance is checked daily against a certified check-weight and the deviation is recorded. This is an example of:
options: A routine performance/calibration verification check
A destructive test
A gravimetric analysis of an unknown sample
A method validation study
questions.correct_answer: A routine performance/calibration verification check
questions.explanation: Daily checks against a known reference weight verify the balance continues to perform within acceptable tolerance between full formal calibrations.

questions.question: Why is document control (version numbering, approval signatures, controlled distribution) important for SOPs in a quality system?
options: To ensure staff always use the current, approved version of a procedure and prevent use of outdated instructions
To make documents harder for staff to find
To increase the number of pages in the quality manual
It is a purely cosmetic requirement with no functional purpose
questions.correct_answer: To ensure staff always use the current, approved version of a procedure and prevent use of outdated instructions
questions.explanation: Document control prevents the use of obsolete or unapproved procedures, ensuring all personnel follow the latest validated version of an SOP.
